clue.text: Terrible wind interrupts middle of meal. Curry perhaps?

indicators.note: interrupts means breaks into the middle of the other piece
middle of means the central letters of the next word are taken

parts.note: its two central letters are used

indicators.note: terrible suggests the letters are mangled into a different order

explanation.surface: Awful flatulence breaks up a dinner, perhaps because of a spicy curry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Terrible' rearranges WIND as DWIN, which 'interrupts' EA, the 'middle of' meal. The curry looks like food, but it is a sound-alike for Edwina Currie, the former British Conservative minister.
explanation.definitionFit: Edwina Currie is a former UK government minister, so a person named Currie is an example of someone with this first name; the question mark flags the punning spelling.

clue.text: The morning after ejecting good Hislop, say, from a royal house

indicators.note: ejecting means throwing out, so a letter is removed from the word

parts.note: the morning after a night's drinking is the hangover
Ian Hislop, editor of Private Eye and a TV panellist, is one example of an Ian

explanation.surface: A hungover morning after throwing the satirist Ian Hislop out of a palace.
explanation.walkthrough: HANGOVER 'ejecting' G gives HANOVER, then IAN; 'say' marks Hislop as one example of someone called Ian. The House of Hanover gave Britain its Georgian kings.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanoverian describes the dynasty of the House of Hanover, the British royal family from George I to Victoria.

clue.text: Overturned legal action about new fool's complaint in hearing

indicators.note: about means the turned word goes round the next pieces
overturned in a down clue means the word is flipped and read from the bottom up

parts.note: a suit is a lawsuit, a legal action
a nit is a fool, short for nitwit

explanation.surface: A court case is overturned regarding a fresh idiot's complaint at a hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: SUIT 'Overturned' gives TIUS, which goes 'about' N + NIT. 'Hearing' looks like a court hearing but means the sense of hearing.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinnitus is a ringing or buzzing in the ears, a medical complaint affecting one's hearing.

clue.text: Fuss follows Kipling novel about Japanese emperor

indicators.note: follows means the word for fuss comes after the reversed title
about means turned round, so the title is read backwards

parts.note: Kim is Rudyard Kipling's novel of 1901
ado means fuss, as in much ado about nothing

explanation.surface: An uproar follows a Kipling book about a Japanese ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: KIM turned 'about' is MIK, and ADO 'follows' it. 'About' looks like 'concerning', but it reverses the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Mikado is an old title used in the West for the Emperor of Japan, as in Gilbert and Sullivan's opera.

clue.text: Discrepancy is holding up male striker?

indicators.note: In a down entry whatever does the holding sits underneath what it supports, so the little word goes below the letter for the man.

parts.note: m = male, the abbreviation on every form you fill in
the clue's own word, taken as it stands and propped up from below
a match is the thing you strike to make a flame

explanation.surface: A discrepancy in the paperwork delaying a male footballer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Male striker' looks like one footballer and is really two separate pieces of the build — and the striker is the thing you strike, not a player.
explanation.definitionFit: A mismatch is a pair of things that fail to agree, which is what a discrepancy is — one noun for the other.

clue.text: OK, USA angry with raw Japanese film-maker

indicators.note: Somebody angry has lost their composure, and letters that lose theirs will not stay in the arrangement the clue hands them over in.

parts.note: five letters of fodder
three more, making the eight the enumeration asks for

explanation.surface: The United States giving grudging approval while furious about something served raw.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all grumbling about food, and there is no hint in it that a director's name is being spelled out. Akira Kurosawa made Rashomon and Seven Samurai.
explanation.definitionFit: Akira Kurosawa was Japan's most internationally famous director, so the definition names him by nationality and trade instead of by name.

clue.text: Eg x, y or z having a range of possible values

definitions.meaning: the letters algebra reaches for when a quantity has not been fixed yet

definitions.text: having a range of possible values
definitions.meaning: a quantity free to take any value across a range, rather than one settled number

explanation.surface: A maths lesson explaining what the letters in an equation stand for.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are mathematical, which is what makes the seam so hard to find: the first names three examples, the second describes the class those examples belong to.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the algebraic symbol standing for an unfixed quantity; the other is the adjective for anything able to take different values.

clue.text: Crash into party

definitions.meaning: to drive hard into something, with the noise that goes with it
a big informal party, as in a fiftieth birthday do

explanation.surface: Somebody blundering uninvited into a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Into' is joinery and nothing more, which is why the three words read as a single action rather than as two senses standing side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a heavy blow or collision; the other is the informal British word for a large party, and the two meanings are unrelated.

clue.text: Regularly observed Neptunian volcano

indicators.note: Watching something regularly means taking it at fixed intervals, and the interval here is one letter in every two.

parts.note: start at the second letter and take every second one after it, right through the word

explanation.surface: An astronomer keeping a regular watch on a volcano out at Neptune.
explanation.walkthrough: Neptune has no volcano of this kind, so the picture is science fiction and the real work is counting letters. Etna is the great cone on Sicily.
explanation.definitionFit: Etna is the huge active volcano in Sicily, so the bare word names the answer by the category it belongs to.

clue.text: Snack wherein raspberries somewhat making a comeback

indicators.note: Only a part of what has just been said is meant, and the part wanted is an unbroken run of letters inside those words.
Something making a comeback returns the way it went, so in an across entry the run has to be read from right to left.

parts.note: six letters standing in a row across the join between the two words, pointing the wrong way

explanation.surface: Raspberries coming back into fashion as something to nibble on.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing has been rearranged here: the letters are already sitting in the clue, facing backwards. A sarnie is what much of Britain informally calls a sandwich.
explanation.definitionFit: A sarnie is British slang for a sandwich, which is the snack meant — the same everyday thing in a chattier register.

clue.text: Angrily attacks plump child

parts.note: a round figure is a plump one
a son is somebody's male child

explanation.surface: A tirade aimed at a chubby youngster.
explanation.walkthrough: To round on somebody is to turn and lay into them with words rather than fists, which is why the definition says angrily rather than violently.
explanation.definitionFit: To round on somebody is to turn and attack them verbally, so 'Angrily attacks' matches both the aggression and the third-person form.

clue.text: Awful magnate uses relief

indicators.note: Something awful has gone badly wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are no longer in the order they were handed to you.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder, exactly the length the enumeration asks for

explanation.surface: A dreadful tycoon helping himself to a relief fund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uses' is where the mechanism hides: it reads as the verb of the sentence about the magnate, and it is really four more letters of fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Assuagement is the easing of pain, grief or hunger, which is what relief names — two abstract nouns for the same softening.

clue.text: English pirate confused with tax exile

indicators.note: A confused thing has its parts muddled together, so the letters beside it are re-laid in an order the clue never gives.

parts.note: e = English, the standard single letter, joining the fodder
six letters of fodder
three more, making ten in all

explanation.surface: A bewildered English pirate tangled up with the taxman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax exile' is the trap: the two words look like one familiar phrase, and only the second of them belongs to the definition — the first is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An expatriate lives outside their own country, so 'exile' is a noun for the same person, though an exile is more often driven out.

clue.text: Rubbish collection of points almost nobody accepts

indicators.note: the nobody word accepts, takes in, the other letters

parts.note: none means nobody

indicators.note: almost means the word loses its last letter

parts.note: S, E, N, S, E are a collection of compass points

explanation.surface: Waste is gathered at points where barely anyone takes it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collection of points' looks like a score tally, but it means compass points: south, east, north, south, east.
explanation.definitionFit: Nonsense means foolish or meaningless talk, which is what rubbish means in its figurative sense.

clue.text: Create classes in biology on vacuous theme

indicators.note: This is a down entry, so a piece sitting on another is written above it and comes first as the answer reads downwards.

parts.note: the groupings a biologist sorts species into, sitting between family and species

indicators.note: A vacuous word has had its insides emptied out, leaving only the letter at each end.

parts.note: the word emptied of its middle, keeping only its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A biology lesson on classification hung on a rather empty topic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Classes' is loose: class is a rank of its own in biological classification, and the groupings the wordplay wants sit several rungs below it.
explanation.definitionFit: To generate something is to bring it into existence, which is what 'Create' asks for — verb for verb, with no shade of difference.

clue.text: Outdo Kew Gardens, ultimately plugging trim variety of primula

indicators.note: plugging means filling a gap inside the other piece

parts.note: to clip is to trim

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so the final letter of each word is used

parts.note: the final letter of each of these three words is taken

explanation.surface: A rival garden trying to beat Kew with a neatly trimmed primrose.
explanation.walkthrough: The ends of Outdo, Kew and Gardens, taken 'ultimately', give OWS, which goes 'plugging' CLIP after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: The cowslip, Primula veris, is a yellow-flowered wild plant of the primrose genus.

clue.text: Track automatically not changed after secure start to Olympics

indicators.note: after means the rearranged word comes after the previous pieces

parts.note: to lock something is to secure it

indicators.note: start to means the first letter of the next word

parts.note: its first letter is taken

indicators.note: changed means the letters of the word are rearranged

explanation.surface: Something left as it was after the safe opening of the Olympic Games.
explanation.walkthrough: LOCK plus O (the 'start to' Olympics) is followed, 'after', by NOT 'changed' into NTO.
explanation.definitionFit: A missile or radar that locks on to a target tracks it automatically, a phrasal verb with that sense.

clue.text: Imminent selection of trains to Retford

indicators.note: A selection of something is a part taken out of it, and the part wanted here is a run of letters standing together.

parts.note: seven letters in a row, running across the ends of these three words

explanation.surface: A departure board listing the next services to Retford.
explanation.walkthrough: Retford is a small Nottinghamshire town, in the clue only because its opening letters complete the run. The railway picture has nothing to do with the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something in store for you is waiting to happen, so 'Imminent' catches the sense of an event already on its way.

clue.text: Updates can't corrupt word-processing technique

indicators.note: A corrupted file has its contents scrambled, and the same thing happens to the letters standing next to the word.

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder once the apostrophe is set aside

explanation.surface: Software updates that stubbornly refuse to install.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Corrupt' does double duty in the picture — corrupted updates are exactly what the surface describes, which is why it never reads as an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Cut and paste is the standard editing move in a word processor: lift the text out and drop it in somewhere else.

clue.text: Shrub split in part

indicators.note: The little word puts one piece inside the other rather than beside it, and that placement is the whole instruction.

parts.note: pt is the everyday shortening of part, as in Pt 1 of a series
to rive something is to split it apart, the verb behind 'riven'

explanation.surface: A garden shrub that has split partway down.
explanation.walkthrough: RIVE is worth banking: it means to tear or split, and it survives mainly in crosswords, old poetry and the word riven.
explanation.definitionFit: Privet is the dense-leaved shrub grown for suburban hedging, so 'Shrub' defines it by the plain category it belongs to.

clue.text: Increasingly bright star Victor wears angora, off and on

indicators.note: wears means is dressed in, so the letter for Victor goes inside the other piece like a body in clothes
off and on means alternately skipping and taking letters

parts.note: every other letter of it is taken, starting from the second
Victor is V in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A rising star named Victor sometimes wears an angora jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: Taking the letters of angora 'off and on' from the second gives NOA, and Victor 'wears' it: V goes inside. A jumper is a sweater.
explanation.definitionFit: A nova is a star that suddenly flares to great brightness before fading, so it grows brighter.

clue.text: Finally evading snake, breathe with effort

indicators.note: Taken finally, a word gives up only its closing letter, and the rest of it plays no part in the build.

parts.note: the closing letter of the second word
an asp is the small viper of Cleopatra's story

explanation.surface: Somebody struggling for breath after narrowly dodging a snake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Finally evading snake' reads as a narrow escape, and the comma is the only sign that 'finally' is an instruction rather than part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: To gasp is to draw breath sharply and with difficulty, which is the laboured breathing the definition describes — verb for verb.

clue.text: Composition of other ranks taken on by Nelson without introduction

indicators.note: To take somebody on is to take them in, so the smaller piece is admitted inside the larger rather than tacked onto it.

parts.note: the admiral's first name was Horatio, docked here of its opening letter
OR is the British army's own term for soldiers below commissioned rank

explanation.surface: Nelson taking on a company of ordinary soldiers without so much as an introduction.
explanation.walkthrough: Nelson is here for his first name rather than his fame, which is why the surface can talk about the navy while the wordplay quietly spells a Georgian Christian name.
explanation.definitionFit: An oratorio is a large sacred work for choir, soloists and orchestra, so 'Composition' names it by its broad musical category.

clue.text: Compete with sides from Nigeria outside northern capital

parts.note: to vie is to compete

indicators.note: outside means the outer letters wrap round the next piece
sides from means the first and last letters of the next word

parts.note: only its outer letters are used

explanation.surface: Rivals take on a team from Nigeria somewhere north of the capital.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sides from' Nigeria are NA, which go 'outside' N, after VIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Vienna is the capital city of Austria.

clue.text: Pop round, given small desire for food

indicators.note: round means turned round, so the short word is read backwards

parts.note: pop and pa are both words for father
petite means small, especially of a woman's build

explanation.surface: Dad pops over, having only a small appetite.
explanation.walkthrough: PA turned 'round' gives AP, then PETITE.
explanation.definitionFit: Appetite is the natural craving or hunger for something to eat.

clue.text: Venerate American patriot Paul

definitions.meaning: to hold in deep respect, the verb used of saints and heroes
the Boston silversmith who rode through the night in 1775 to warn that the British were coming

explanation.surface: Honouring one of the heroes of the American Revolution.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a single instruction to honour a named man, and the seam falls after the first word: one half is the verb, the other is his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the verb for holding something in awe; the other is Paul Revere, whose surname happens to be spelled the same way.
